title: Rejecting Ideas and Proposals Because of the Source
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article names 'reactive devaluation,' the tendency to dismiss an idea simply because of who proposed it, as a common and largely instinctive bias that undermines objective decision-making. It explains that leaders naturally question the motives of people they distrust, which lets them justify dismissing proposals without engaging their actual merits, ultimately leaving decisions less informed. The piece recommends a specific countermeasure: mentally attributing a disliked person's idea to a trusted colleague before evaluating it, to separate the proposal's substance from feelings about its source.
points: 'Reactive devaluation,' dismissing ideas based on who proposed them, is named as a common cognitive bias.
The bias is described as largely instinctive, reinforcing in-group identity by favoring trusted sources.
A leader known to exhibit this bias risks damaging their own credibility with observers.
The recommended countermeasure: mentally attribute the idea to a trusted colleague before evaluating it.
quotes: The real danger lies in the common bias of rejecting any idea or proposal that comes from a given source.
People expect leaders and decision-makers to operate above their personal feelings and to maintain an impartial and objective lens on all ideas and proposals, no matter where they emanate from.
Yet, this bias, known by the fancy psychological name of reactive devaluation, is tremendously common.
In fact, in many cases, the best leaders may pretend the proposal came from a trusted colleague or third party so they can evaluate it fairly.
Do your best to fight this bias. It has nothing to do with changing your mind about the person, and everything to do with changing your mind about yourself.
